title: "Part 2 – The claim and its estimand"
---
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Slides.** [Open the deck at this part](../../slides/housing-one-day-open-science.html#/part-2-the-claim-and-its-estimand){target="_blank"} in its own tab, or follow it on the [slides page](slides.qmd).
:::

Part 2 reads the paper, sets out what the five Multi100 analysts did with its claim, and argues that analysts who look as though they disagree are often answering different questions. It then gives you the tool for saying which question you are answering, the estimand statement, and you write one for the claim before lunch. The part takes ninety minutes.

## 1. The paper

**On the slides.** The slides present the paper of the original authors (OAs): the question that it asks, the design, the email word for word, what came back for each of the six names, and the four outcomes that were coded. They end on the claim as SCORE selected it, with its two ellipses.

## 2. The five analysts

**On the slides.** The five Multi100 analysts are placed by their gaps in percentage points. A table then sets out what each of them did, with five different questions behind two different verdicts.

## 3. Estimands

**On the slides.** Two studies are set beside our five. The red-card estimates return as a single row, with the four estimands that the twenty-nine teams were in fact pursuing and the spread that collapses once the estimand is fixed. The slides then ask what under-specified research questions mean for the reading of many-analysts studies, and present the steps from a theoretical to an empirical estimand that Lundberg and colleagues set out.

## 4. The estimand statement and the graph

**On the slides.** You write the estimand statement in the chat, hold it, and send it with the rest of the class when the facilitator says go. The slides then draw the causal graph of the experiment, show why comparing greetings among the replies conditions on a consequence of the name, and end on what changes when every delivered email is counted.

## 5. The R tutorial (optional)

**On the slides**, if the class wants it. The tutorial puts R in one slide, then covers reading and inspecting the data, the verbs that work on rows and columns, tables and tests, model formulas, a plot, causal graphs in R, and the error messages that you are most likely to meet.

## 6. Task 2 – The data

[Open the browser lab at Task 2](../../cases/housing/lab.qmd#task-2-data){.btn .btn-primary target="_blank"}

Count the emails that bounced, the replies, the replies with a greeting code and the greetings by name, for each name. Write the estimand statement with every bracket filled, saying which emails you count. If there is time, finish the causal graph in the [graph cell](../../cases/housing/lab.qmd#task-2-estimand-and-graph). Finish with two sentences, one on what a comparison among the replies conditions on and one on what counting every delivered email changes.

**By the end of the part** you have the estimand behind the claim written in one sentence, and two sentences on why the choice of which emails to count changes the question. Both go into the preregistration block of Part 4.
